```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This article describes how `inkr` decides which declaration wins when several
rules set the same property. The complete rules are part of the language
specification; here they are shown by example.

```{r}
library(inkr)
```

## Selectors

| Selector | Matches an element when |
|----------|-------------------------|
| `*` | always |
| `Button` | `type` is `"Button"` |
| `#save` | `id` is `"save"` |
| `.primary` | `classes` contains `"primary"` |
| `:focus` | `states` contains `"focus"` (any valid name works) |
| `Button.primary:focus` | all of the above hold for the same element |
| `Container Button` | some ancestor is a `Container` (descendant) |
| `Container > Button` | the direct parent is a `Container` (child) |
| `Button, Input` | either selector matches |

Selectors are matched right to left against the chain of parents. Identifiers
are case-sensitive.

## Specificity

`ink_specificity()` returns the tuple `c(id, class, type)`: ids, then classes
and pseudo-classes, then types. `*` and combinators count nothing. Tuples are
compared lexicographically, never as a weighted sum, so one id always beats any
number of classes.

```{r}
selector <- function(text) {
  ink_parse(paste(text, "{ color: red; }"))$statements[[1]]$selectors$selectors[[1]]
}
ink_specificity(selector("Button"))
ink_specificity(selector("Button.primary:focus"))
ink_specificity(selector("#save"))
ink_specificity(selector("Container Button.primary"))
```

## Variables

Variables are defined at the top level with `$name: value;` and are resolved
when the stylesheet is compiled. A property value is typed, not a string:

```{r}
sheet <- ink_compile(ink_parse("
  $accent: #7c3aed;
  Button { background: $accent; }
"))
sheet
sheet$rules[[1]]$declarations[[1]]$value$r
```

## Resolving conflicting declarations

For each property independently:

1. the declaration with the higher specificity wins;
2. with equal specificity, the later rule wins;
3. within one rule, the later declaration wins.

The example below has four rules that set `color`.

```{r}
sheet <- ink_compile(ink_parse("
  Screen   { color: green; }
  Button   { color: white; }
  .primary { color: blue; }
  #save    { color: yellow; }
"))
screen <- ink_element("Screen", id = "main")
panel <- ink_element("Container", parent = screen)
button <- ink_element("Button", id = "save", classes = "primary", parent = panel)

ink_match(sheet, button)
```

`Screen` does not apply to the button (it is not a `Screen`), so three rules
compete. Their specificities are `(0, 0, 1)`, `(0, 1, 0)` and `(1, 0, 0)`, and
the id selector wins even though the rules before it come first in the source.

```{r}
ink_compute(sheet, button)$values$color
ink_explain(sheet, button, "color")
```

Equal specificity is decided by source order:

```{r}
sheet <- ink_compile(ink_parse("
  .a { color: red; }
  .b { color: blue; }
"))
element <- ink_element("Label", classes = c("a", "b"))
ink_compute(sheet, element)$values$color
```

For a selector list such as `Button, #save`, the specificity used is that of
the most specific selector that actually matched. Only one stylesheet is
considered: there are no other origins, inline styles or `!important`.

## Inheritance

For every registered property, `ink_compute()` uses, in order:

1. the winning declaration, if any (`inherit` and `initial` are resolved
   here);
2. otherwise the parent's computed value, if the property inherits (`color`
   and `text-style` among the built-in properties);
3. otherwise the registry's initial value.

```{r}
sheet <- ink_compile(ink_parse("
  Screen { color: green; padding: 2; }
"))
screen <- ink_element("Screen")
label <- ink_element("Label", parent = ink_element("Container", parent = screen))
style <- ink_compute(sheet, label)
style$values$color
style$values$padding
style$provenance$color$origin
style$provenance$padding$origin
```

The label inherits `color` through a container that declares nothing, but not
`padding`, which does not inherit. `inherit` forces inheritance for any
property and `initial` always gives the registry's initial value.

## Explaining a value

`ink_explain()` runs the same cascade as `ink_compute()` and records what
happened, so it cannot disagree with the computed style. For an inherited
value, the explanation traces the chain of elements:

```{r}
ink_explain(sheet, label, "color")
```

The result is structured data (`value`, `origin`, `winner`, `candidates`,
`resolution`); printing is only a view of it. See `?ink_explain`.

## Style sessions

A session owns an element tree and caches computed styles, for trees that are
queried repeatedly and changed a little at a time. It returns exactly what the
stateless functions return.

```{r}
sheet <- ink_compile(ink_parse("
  Screen { color: white; }
  .active Button { color: yellow; }
"))
session <- ink_session(sheet)
ink_session_set(session, key = "root", type = "Screen")
ink_session_set(session, key = "panel", type = "Container", parent_key = "root")
ink_session_set(session, key = "button", type = "Button", parent_key = "panel")

ink_session_compute(session, "button")$values$color

ink_session_set(session, "panel", classes = "active")
ink_session_compute(session, "button")$values$color
ink_session_stats(session)
```

Changing a node drops the cached styles of that node and all its descendants;
other branches keep their caches. See `?ink_session`.
